slides.title: Memory architectures
slides.caption: Memory is what an agent keeps between tasks. This section looks at how memories are built and scored. It asks how far the scores are from what an enterprise needs.

slides.title: What we will cover
slides.caption: Six pages. Why memory needs its own section, six ways to build one, and how memory is scored. Then long context, the ten-million-token question, and what we measured.

slides.title: An agent forgets when the task ends
slides.caption: A model reads text and writes text. An agent is a system that uses a model to do a job. When the job ends, the model keeps nothing.

slides.title: That something is its memory
slides.caption: Memory is what is built around the model so the agent can recall. It is a store, an index, and a way to bring the right piece back.

slides.title: A crowded field
slides.caption: By September 2026 there are more than thirty named memory systems and four managed cloud services. Six survey taxonomies and ten new benchmarks. Almost none of their scores compare.

slides.title: Two facts decide everything
slides.caption: Every memory architecture is placed by what it stores and by when a model runs. Those two choices fix what can be recalled and what it costs.

slides.title: Every high score is small
slides.caption: Every memory score above 90 percent was earned on a conversation of 16 thousand to 115 thousand tokens. That fits inside one call to a modern model.

slides.title: Ten million tokens
slides.caption: Ten million tokens is a little more than one year of one worker's received mail and chat. An enterprise memory workload starts there and grows.

slides.title: At ten million, the best result
slides.caption: One public benchmark reaches ten million tokens. There, plain long context scores 0.10 and retrieval 0.25. The authors' own memory design scores 0.27 on a scale of 0 to 1.

slides.title: Vendor numbers at ten million are unchecked
slides.caption: Three vendors have published their own ten-million-token scores. Each used its own judge and harness. None is comparable to the paper, and none has been reproduced.

slides.title: Three rules for every number
slides.caption: Vendor numbers are flagged and never ranked against each other. Independently measured numbers sit in their own rows. Retrieval scores and answer scores never share a table.

slides.title: Six pages in this section
slides.caption: The six pages: the taxonomy, the benchmarks, long context, the ten-million-token question, what we measured, and the sources.

slides.title: The question is open
slides.caption: No independently run, published result shows any memory architecture or long-context model answering well over a single ten-million-token corpus. The section ends on that gap.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.caption: Memory is built by what is stored and when a model runs. Every high score is on a small test. Ten million tokens is the floor, and nothing solid has been shown there.
